name: 54gene
one_liner: African genomics company building a biobank of African DNA for drug discovery
story: 54gene raised about $45M to sequence under-represented African genomes for pharma partners and expanded into COVID testing and a diagnostics arm. Its founder-CEO stepped down in 2022 amid layoffs and a valuation cut of over $100M, and the company wound down in 2023 while seeking buyers for its biobank.

name: Dash
one_liner: Pan-African wallet linking mobile money and bank accounts across countries
story: Dash pitched itself as the 'Alipay for Africa' and reportedly raised $86.1M in five years (TechCrunch counted ~$50M including $20M venture debt), claiming $1B in transactions. The Bank of Ghana flagged it in 2022 for operating without approval; the founder was suspended in 2023 over alleged financial impropriety (allegations, not court findings) and the company shut in October 2023.

name: Lipa Later
one_liner: Kenyan buy-now-pay-later provider for electronics and retail purchases
story: Lipa Later raised a $12M pre-Series A (equity plus debt) in 2022 to expand BNPL into Tanzania, Ghana and Nigeria, part of over $15M total. Lending needs constant fresh capital; after failing to raise in 2024 it could not pay staff and suppliers and entered administration in March 2025.

name: Copia Global
one_liner: Agent-based e-commerce for rural and middle-income African consumers
story: Copia sold groceries and household goods to rural Kenyans through a network of local agents and raised over $100M, including a $50M Series C in 2022. It exited Uganda in April 2023 cutting 350+ jobs, then Copia Global filed for administration in 2024 when it could not raise on acceptable terms.

name: Sendy
one_liner: Kenyan on-demand delivery and freight marketplace for businesses
story: Sendy matched businesses with motorbike and truck drivers and raised over $26M, including a $20M Series B co-led by Toyota Tsusho. It cut staff twice in 2022 and shut its supply (food distribution) pivot, then ran out of money and entered administration with an asset sale in 2023.

name: Okra
one_liner: Open-banking API connecting Nigerian bank accounts to apps (Plaid for Africa)
story: Okra pioneered open-banking APIs in Nigeria before the central bank's open-banking rules went live, raising about $16.5M. After a 2024 pivot into cloud services it closed in May 2025 and returned roughly $4-5.5M of unused cash to investors.

name: ORide
one_liner: Opera-backed motorbike ride-hailing service in Lagos
story: ORide was part of Opera's OPay super-app bet in Nigeria, funded by $170M raised in 2019, and flooded Lagos with subsidised bike rides against Gokada and Max. Lagos banned commercial motorbike hailing in most of the city in early 2020 and ORide shut in mid-2020, while OPay itself pivoted to payments and became a $2B unicorn.

name: Kune Food
one_liner: Nairobi cloud kitchen selling affordable ready-to-eat meals by delivery
story: Kune raised a $1M pre-seed (with a launch PR controversy over its founder's comments on Kenyan food culture) and ran cloud kitchens in Nairobi. When a promised follow-on investment was withdrawn in 2022 it ran out of money and shut after 10 months, laying off 90 staff.

name: Thepeer
one_liner: API letting Nigerian fintech wallets send money to each other
story: Thepeer raised a $2.1M seed in 2022 to connect wallets across Nigerian fintechs. Its founders said they never found product-market fit, acquisition talks failed, and it shut in April 2024, returning remaining capital to investors.

name: Edukoya
one_liner: Live online tutoring and exam-prep app for African secondary students
story: Edukoya raised a record $3.5M pre-seed in 2021 for live synchronous tutoring. Poor connectivity, device access and low disposable income stopped it scaling; after failed merger and pivot talks it shut in February 2025 and returned capital to investors.

name: Gro Intelligence
one_liner: AI platform forecasting crop supply and climate risk for agribusiness and governments
story: Kenyan-born founder Sara Menker built Gro (offices in Nairobi and New York) into a high-profile agri-data platform with roughly $120M raised. After emergency funding and 60% layoffs in March 2024, the board replaced the founder and the company shut in June 2024 after failing to find a buyer.

name: M-Pesa South Africa (Vodacom)
one_liner: Vodacom's attempt to bring Kenya's M-Pesa mobile money to South Africa
story: Vodacom launched M-Pesa in South Africa in 2010 and relaunched it in 2014 with a Visa card, targeting 10M users. It reached only about 1M registered and 76,000 active users, because South Africans already had bank branches and cards and regulation was stricter than Kenya's; Vodacom shut it on 30 June 2016.

name: Twiga Foods
one_liner: B2B platform sourcing produce from farmers and supplying Nairobi's informal kiosks
story: Twiga raised over $160M (reports range to $185M) to digitise fresh-food supply to Kenyan mama-mboga kiosks, including a $50M Series C led by Creadev. It cut a third of staff in 2022, moved asset-light in 2025 amid allegations of a 'soft liquidation', and the operating entity entered administration in August 2026.

name: Konga
one_liner: Nigerian online marketplace that raced Jumia to be the Amazon of Africa
story: Backed by Naspers and Kinnevik (reported totals $78-108M), Konga was valued at $383M in 2015 while burning cash against Rocket Internet's Jumia. In 2018 both investors sold to local electronics firm Zinox for an undisclosed price that Naspers filings imply was at most ~$32M, booking a loss.

name: M-Pesa (Safaricom)
one_liner: SMS-based mobile money service run by Safaricom that became Kenya's default payment rail
story: Safaricom (part-owned by Vodafone) launched M-Pesa in 2007 after a UK-aid-funded pilot, letting people send money by SMS and cash in or out at agents. In a country with few bank branches and a dominant telco it spread fast, but the same product failed in South Africa (shut 2016) where banks were already everywhere.

name: Flutterwave
one_liner: Payments infrastructure letting businesses accept and send money across Africa
story: Flutterwave (YC 2016) built rails for merchants to accept cards, bank transfers and mobile money across dozens of African currencies. It became a unicorn in 2021 and was valued at $3B in a $250M Series D in 2022, Africa's most valuable startup at the time, though it later faced regulatory probes in Kenya and down-market pressure.

name: Paystack
one_liner: Developer-friendly online payments API for Nigerian businesses
story: Paystack (YC W16) made it easy for Nigerian merchants to accept cards online and was backed by Stripe in its Series A. Stripe bought it in October 2020 for over $200M, the biggest African startup acquisition at the time, after only ~$10M raised.

name: OPay
one_liner: Opera-founded mobile wallet and POS agent network in Nigeria and Egypt
story: OPay launched as part of Opera's Nigerian super-app with ride-hailing (ORide), food and logistics. After Lagos banned bike-hailing in 2020 it shut the side bets and focused on payments and POS agents, then raised $400M at $2B led by SoftBank Vision Fund 2 in 2021.

name: Moniepoint
one_liner: Payments and banking platform for Nigerian small businesses and POS agents
story: Started as TeamApt building bank software, Moniepoint pivoted to POS terminals and business accounts for Nigerian merchants and agents. It says it processes over 800M transactions a month while profitable, and its $110M Series C in 2024 (with Google's Africa fund) valued it at $1B.

name: Wave
one_liner: Low-fee mobile money app charging a flat 1% to send in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire

rounds.lead: Sequoia Heritage, Founders Fund, Ribbit Capital, Stripe

story: Wave attacked telco mobile money (Orange Money) with free cash-in/out and a flat 1% send fee, forcing Orange to cut prices. Its $200M Series A at $1.7B in 2021 was then the largest Series A for an African fintech, making it Francophone Africa's first unicorn.

name: Andela
one_liner: Marketplace placing vetted African (now global) software engineers in remote roles
story: Andela started by training developers in Lagos and placing them with US companies, then went fully remote and global in 2020, closing its African campuses. Remote work demand drove a $200M Series E led by SoftBank at $1.5B in 2021.

name: Jumia
one_liner: Rocket Internet's pan-African Amazon-style marketplace
story: Rocket Internet launched Jumia in Lagos in 2012 and rolled it across Africa with MTN and other backers. It listed on the NYSE in April 2019 at about $1.1B, the first African tech IPO in New York, but has never been profitable, and in December 2023 it shut its food delivery arm in all 7 markets.

name: Interswitch
one_liner: Nigeria's payment switch and Verve card scheme
story: Interswitch connected Nigerian banks' ATMs and cards from 2002 and launched the Verve card scheme. Visa took a minority stake (reported ~20% for ~$200M) in 2019, valuing it at about $1B and making it one of Africa's first fintech unicorns; its long-planned IPO has repeatedly slipped.

name: TymeBank
one_liner: South African digital bank onboarding customers through supermarket kiosks
story: TymeBank launched in 2019 with kiosks in Pick n Pay and Boxer stores, signing up millions of low-income South Africans, and expanded to the Philippines as GoTyme. Brazil's Nubank led a $250M Series D in December 2024 at a $1.5B valuation.

name: Babylon Health
one_liner: AI symptom checker and video-GP service that ran NHS practices and US value-based care
story: Babylon raised a record $550M in 2019 and went public via SPAC in 2021 at about $4.2B, promising AI-driven primary care. Losses from taking on full risk for US patients under value-based contracts ballooned while its AI claims drew scrutiny; in 2023 its US arm went bankrupt and the UK business was sold for a nominal sum.

name: Cazoo
one_liner: Buy a used car fully online and get it delivered to your door
story: Zoopla founder Alex Chesterman launched Cazoo in 2019 as a UK Carvana and listed via SPAC in 2021 at about $7B, then expanded into five EU countries. Holding thousands of cars, heavy marketing and rising rates produced huge losses; it retreated from Europe in 2022, its shares fell over 99% and it entered administration in 2024.

name: Arrival
one_liner: Electric vans and buses built in low-cost 'microfactories'
story: Arrival listed via SPAC in 2021 and briefly hit a ~$13B market value on a UPS order and its microfactory concept, without having produced vehicles at scale. Production targets slipped repeatedly, cash ran out, its UK units entered administration in 2024 and assets were sold off.

name: Bulb Energy
one_liner: Cheap, simple green-energy supplier for UK households
story: Bulb grew to about 1.7M customers by undercutting incumbents, but it had not hedged wholesale energy and the UK price cap stopped it passing on costs. When gas prices spiked in 2021 it collapsed into special administration, the largest UK state rescue since RBS, and its customers were transferred to Octopus Energy in 2022.

name: Octopus Energy
one_liner: Green energy supplier running on its own Kraken billing and operations platform
story: Founded the same year as Bulb, Octopus built its own Kraken software and licensed it to other utilities, and survived the 2021 energy crisis that killed dozens of UK suppliers. It absorbed Bulb's customers in 2022 and became the UK's largest household supplier, raising $800M at $7.8B in 2023.

name: Made.com
one_liner: Online designer furniture made to order in Asia and shipped direct to buyers
story: Made.com listed in London in June 2021 at £775M (~$1.07B) after a lockdown sales boom. Container shipping costs from Asia soared and demand fell, it failed to raise more money and collapsed in November 2022, with Next buying the brand for £3.4M.

name: Powa Technologies
one_liner: Mobile payments and 'click to buy' commerce platform
story: Powa's founder claimed a $2.7B valuation in 2014 and announced big partnerships for its mobile payments and PowaTag products, but revenue never materialised. It went into administration in February 2016, one of the UK's biggest tech collapses of its era.

name: Britishvolt
one_liner: Startup planning a £3.8B EV battery gigafactory in northern England
story: Britishvolt promised a £3.8B gigafactory at Blyth with government support but had no proven cell technology or anchor customer. It failed to raise funding as markets turned and entered administration in January 2023; Australia's Recharge Industries bought the remains for about £8.6M.

name: Wonga
one_liner: Algorithmic short-term payday lender approving loans in minutes
story: Wonga became the UK's best-known payday lender with automated underwriting and high interest rates. After the FCA capped costs and forced it in 2014 to write off £220M of loans for 330,000 customers, a flood of compensation claims pushed it into administration in August 2018.

name: Boo.com
one_liner: Dot-com era online fashion store with 3D product views in 18 countries
story: Swedish founders raised about $135M from backers including JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Bernard Arnault and launched simultaneously in many countries with a heavy, slow website when most users were on dial-up. It burned through the money in about six months and was liquidated in May 2000; online fashion later worked for Zalando and ASOS once broadband and logistics existed.

name: Blippar
one_liner: Augmented-reality app letting brands make products and ads interactive
story: Blippar was valued around $1.5B in 2016, one of the UK's first unicorns, selling AR campaigns to brands and pivoting toward visual search. Revenue stayed small, a shareholder dispute blocked new funding and it went into administration in December 2018.

name: Builder.ai
one_liner: 'AI-powered' platform promising to assemble custom apps like ordering a pizza
story: Builder.ai raised over $450M, including from Microsoft and Qatar's sovereign fund, marketing AI that would build software while relying heavily on human developers. In 2025 reports that it had overstated sales led a lender to seize cash, and it filed for insolvency in May 2025.

name: Greensill Capital
one_liner: Supply-chain finance firm packaging invoices into investment funds
story: Greensill advanced cash against invoices (and future receivables) and sold the loans through Credit Suisse funds worth about $10B, backed by SoftBank's ~$1.5B investment. When its credit insurer refused to renew cover in March 2021 it collapsed into insolvency, sparking investigations and a lobbying scandal involving former UK PM David Cameron.

name: Pollen
one_liner: Group travel and music-event experiences sold through creators and influencers
story: Pollen raised a $150M Series C in 2021 betting on a post-COVID boom in festival and group-travel experiences. Heavy cash burn, mass layoffs and a scandal over taking staff and customer money without consent preceded its collapse into administration in August 2022.

name: Hopin
one_liner: Virtual events platform that boomed during COVID lockdowns
story: Hopin went from founding to a $7.75B valuation in about two years as conferences moved online, raising roughly $1B and buying multiple startups. When in-person events returned demand collapsed; in 2023 it sold its events business to RingCentral for $15M upfront (up to $50M), under 1% of its peak value.

name: Graphcore
one_liner: AI processor (IPU) startup challenging Nvidia GPUs
story: Graphcore raised about $710M and hit a $2.77B valuation in 2020 with a new AI chip architecture. Nvidia's CUDA software ecosystem kept customers on GPUs, a Microsoft cloud deal faded, and SoftBank bought it in 2024 for an undisclosed sum reported to be well below the capital raised.

name: Farfetch
one_liner: Online luxury fashion marketplace aggregating boutiques worldwide
story: Portuguese founder José Neves built Farfetch in London with engineering in Porto and listed on the NYSE in 2018 at about $6.2B; its value peaked near $23B in 2021. Costly acquisitions and losses as luxury demand cooled left it near insolvency, and in December 2023 Coupang rescued it with a $500M loan that wiped out shareholders.

name: Citymapper
one_liner: Public-transport journey planner app for big cities
story: Citymapper became a favourite transit app in London and dozens of cities but struggled to monetise, trying its own bus routes and a travel pass. It was acquired by Via in 2023 for an undisclosed sum, while rivals Waze and Moovit had sold to Google and Intel for about $1B each.

name: Truphone
one_liner: Global mobile network and eSIM provider for travellers and IoT
story: Truphone was an early eSIM and international mobile network largely funded by investors linked to Roman Abramovich. After UK sanctions on Abramovich in 2022 froze its funding and customers, the business was sold in September 2022 for £1.

name: Purplebricks
one_liner: Online estate agent charging a fixed fee instead of commission
story: Purplebricks listed on AIM in 2015 and reached a market value around £1.4B in 2018 with Axel Springer investing £125M. Expansion to the US and Australia failed and was shut in 2019, UK share stalled, and in 2023 the company was sold to Strike for £1.

name: OneWeb
one_liner: Low-earth-orbit satellite constellation for global broadband
story: OneWeb raised about $3.4B, largely from SoftBank, to build a LEO internet constellation ahead of SpaceX's Starlink. When SoftBank refused more money at the start of COVID it filed for Chapter 11 in March 2020; the UK government and Bharti bought it for $1B and it later merged with Eutelsat.

name: Railsr
one_liner: Banking-as-a-service APIs letting brands launch cards and accounts
story: Railsr (formerly Railsbank) grew fast in the embedded-finance boom, providing accounts and cards to fintech brands. As fintech clients cut back and funding dried up, it entered administration in March 2023 and was sold via pre-pack to a consortium led by D Squared Capital.

name: Getir (UK, EU and US operations)
one_liner: Getir's 10-minute grocery delivery expansion outside Turkey
story: Getir launched in London in January 2021 and spread to the Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and the US, buying rival Gorillas in 2022. High wages, low order density and price competition made dark stores unprofitable; it quit France, Spain, Italy and Portugal in 2023 and the UK, Germany, Netherlands and US in April 2024, cutting thousands of jobs to refocus on Turkey.

name: Revolut
one_liner: Multi-currency card and app that grew into a global financial super-app
story: Revolut started with fee-free foreign exchange cards for travellers and stacked on trading, crypto and business accounts across dozens of countries. It was valued at $33B in 2021, $45B in a 2024 secondary and about $75B in 2025, and won a restricted UK banking licence in 2024 after years of regulatory delays.

name: Ocado
one_liner: Online-only supermarket with robotic warehouses, later licensed to grocers worldwide
story: Founded in 2000 by ex-Goldman bankers just as Webvan was collapsing in the US, Ocado partnered with Waitrose for products and spent a decade building automated central warehouses in one dense market. It listed in London in 2010 at about £937M (~$1.45B), then sold its robotics platform to grocers like Kroger from 2018.

name: Deliveroo
one_liner: Restaurant food delivery app using self-employed riders
story: Deliveroo won the UK and several cities by signing restaurants others did not deliver for, but exited Germany (2019), Spain (2021), the Netherlands and Australia (2022) where local leaders were entrenched. It IPO'd in 2021 at £7.6B (~$10.5B), traded far below that, and DoorDash bought it in 2025 for £2.9B (~$3.9B).

name: Deliveroo Spain
one_liner: Deliveroo's restaurant delivery operation in Spain
story: Deliveroo entered Spain in 2015 but stayed a distant player behind homegrown Glovo and Just Eat. When Spain's 2021 'Ley Rider' required riders to be employees, Deliveroo decided it could not reach scale and left the country in November 2021, while Glovo stayed and fought.

name: Deliveroo Germany
one_liner: Deliveroo's restaurant delivery operation in Germany
story: Deliveroo launched in Berlin in 2015 but Germany consolidated into one dominant player when Takeaway.com bought Delivery Hero's German brands (Lieferheld, Pizza.de, Foodora) in 2018. With Lieferando owning the market, Deliveroo pulled out of Germany in August 2019.

name: Wise
one_liner: Cheap, transparent international money transfers (formerly TransferWise)
story: Estonian founders Kristo Käärmann and Taavet Hinrikus built TransferWise to avoid hidden bank FX mark-ups by matching flows between countries. It was profitable before going public and did a direct listing in London in 2021 at about £8.75B (~$11B).

name: DeepMind
one_liner: AI research lab building general-purpose learning algorithms
story: Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman founded DeepMind in London with early backers including Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Google bought it in January 2014 for a reported ~£400M (~$500M+); it went on to build AlphaGo and AlphaFold, which won a Nobel Prize in 2024.

name: Darktrace
one_liner: Self-learning AI that detects cyber threats inside company networks
story: Darktrace sold AI anomaly detection to enterprises and listed in London in April 2021 at about £1.7B (~$2.3B). Despite short-seller criticism of its accounting, Thoma Bravo took it private in 2024 for about $5.3B.

name: Busuu
one_liner: Language-learning app with native-speaker community feedback
story: Busuu was founded in Madrid in 2008 by Bernhard Niesner and Adrian Hilti and moved to London, growing a freemium language app where native speakers correct learners. Chegg bought it in 2021 for $436M, while US rival Duolingo went public the same year.

name: Zalando
one_liner: Online shoe and fashion retailer with free delivery and returns, started as a Zappos copy
story: Backed by the Samwer brothers' Rocket Internet, Zalando cloned Zappos for Germany in 2008 and expanded across Europe with free returns and local payment methods like pay-on-invoice. It listed in Frankfurt in 2014 at about €5.3B (~$7B) and became Europe's largest online fashion platform.

name: Delivery Hero
one_liner: Global food-delivery group built by buying local leaders in 70+ countries
story: Delivery Hero grew by acquisition: Yemeksepeti (Turkey, $589M), Talabat (Gulf), Woowa (Korea) and a majority of Glovo (Spain). It listed in Frankfurt in 2017 at about €4.4B (~$5B), but sold its own German brands to Takeaway.com in 2018 and later lost money on many expansions.

name: HelloFresh
one_liner: Subscription meal-kit boxes with recipes and pre-portioned ingredients
story: Rocket Internet-backed HelloFresh launched in Berlin in 2011 and expanded into the US and a dozen markets, outlasting US pioneer Blue Apron. It listed in Frankfurt in 2017 at about €1.7B (~$1.9B) and boomed during COVID, while Blue Apron was sold for $103M in 2023.

name: N26
one_liner: Mobile-only bank account with a German banking licence passported across the EU
story: N26 got a German banking licence and grew across the eurozone, reaching a $9B valuation in 2021. It left the UK in 2020 after Brexit and the US in January 2022, and German regulator BaFin capped its customer growth in 2021 over anti-money-laundering failings.

name: N26 US
one_liner: N26's mobile bank account offering in the United States
story: N26 launched in the US in 2019 through a partner bank, without its own US licence, into a market already crowded with Chime, Varo and big banks' apps. It closed US accounts in January 2022 to focus on Europe, having already quit the UK in 2020.

name: Flix (FlixBus)
one_liner: Asset-light intercity bus network where partners own the buses and Flix runs brand, pricing and tech
story: FlixBus launched right after Germany deregulated long-distance buses in 2013, letting local operators run green-branded buses while Flix handled booking and pricing. It consolidated Europe, bought Greyhound in the US in 2021 and raised $650M at about $3B the same year.

name: Auto1 Group
one_liner: Used-car wholesale marketplace for dealers, later adding online retail (Autohero)
story: Auto1 bought cars from consumers and resold them to dealers across Europe within days, avoiding long inventory risk, before launching consumer site Autohero. It listed in Frankfurt in February 2021 at about €8.3B (~$9.8B) and survived the used-car downturn that killed Cazoo and Vroom.

name: BioNTech
one_liner: mRNA immunotherapy company that co-developed the first approved COVID-19 vaccine
story: Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci spent a decade on mRNA cancer therapies, backed by the Strüngmann family office, and listed on Nasdaq in October 2019 at about $3.4B. Partnering with Pfizer in 2020 it delivered the first approved COVID-19 vaccine and its market value briefly topped $100B in 2021; it later bought InstaDeep.

name: StudiVZ
one_liner: German student social network modelled on Facebook
story: StudiVZ copied Facebook's design for German-speaking students before Facebook launched in German, and publisher Holtzbrinck bought it in January 2007 for about €85M (~$116M). Once Facebook localised, users left; the network shrank for a decade and filed for insolvency in 2017.

name: Personio
one_liner: All-in-one HR and payroll software for small and mid-sized European companies
story: Personio targeted European SMEs that were too small for Workday but faced complex local labour and payroll rules. Its 2022 round valued it at $8.5B, making it one of Germany's most valuable software startups.

name: Wefox
one_liner: Digital insurance platform combining broker network and its own insurer
story: Wefox raised over $1B to digitise insurance distribution in Europe, reaching a $4.5B valuation in 2022. Heavy losses led to the founder-CEO stepping down in 2023 and in 2024 it sold off country units and needed an emergency recapitalisation.

name: Gorillas
one_liner: 10-minute grocery delivery from dark stores with employed riders
story: Gorillas became a unicorn in about nine months and raised around $1.3B, expanding to 60+ cities in Europe and New York during the zero-rate era. Rider strikes, low order values and costly dark stores burned cash; it exited several countries in 2022 and Getir bought it in December 2022 in an all-stock deal reported at about $1.2B, below its capital raised.

name: Volocopter
one_liner: Multicopter electric air taxi for short urban flights
story: Volocopter aimed to fly air taxis at the 2024 Paris Olympics but missed certification and the demo. It filed for insolvency in December 2024 after failing to raise more and was bought in early 2025 by China's Wanfeng group (owner of Diamond Aircraft) for a small sum.

name: Lilium
one_liner: Electric vertical take-off jet for regional air-taxi routes
story: Lilium listed via SPAC in 2021 at about $3.3B with a novel ducted-fan jet that had not yet been certified. It repeatedly missed milestones, filed for insolvency in October 2024 after the German government refused a €50M loan guarantee, revived briefly, then ceased operations in February 2025 when a rescue deal collapsed.

name: Wirecard
one_liner: Payment processor that rose into the DAX before a €1.9B accounting fraud
story: Wirecard replaced Commerzbank in Germany's DAX index in 2018 at a market value around €24B (~$28B). After years of FT reporting dismissed by regulators, auditors could not find €1.9B of cash in June 2020; the company filed for insolvency within days and its CEO was arrested.

name: Sono Motors
one_liner: Affordable solar-panelled electric car (the Sion), funded by pre-orders
story: Sono gathered tens of thousands of reservations and community funding for the Sion and listed on Nasdaq in 2021. Without the capital to reach mass production it cancelled the car in early 2023 and filed for insolvency in May 2023, keeping only a small solar-kit business for buses.

name: Infarm
one_liner: Modular vertical farms inside supermarkets and urban hubs
story: Infarm put vertical farms in supermarkets across Europe, the US and Japan and became a unicorn with a $200M round in 2021. When energy prices spiked after 2022 its unit economics broke; it exited most markets, laid off most staff and its operating units went insolvent in 2023, mirroring US failures like AeroFarms.

name: Wimdu
one_liner: Rocket Internet's Airbnb clone for European apartment rentals
story: Rocket Internet launched Wimdu in 2011 with a $90M Series A, then one of Europe's largest, to beat Airbnb to Europe. Airbnb responded by buying another German clone and expanding aggressively; Wimdu merged with 9flats in 2016 and shut in 2018 amid Berlin's short-term rental restrictions.

name: Nuri (formerly Bitwala)
one_liner: Mobile bank account combining euro banking with bitcoin trading
story: Bitwala rebranded as Nuri in 2020 and grew to roughly half a million customers by mixing a bank account (via partner Solarisbank) with bitcoin. When crypto prices crashed and fundraising froze in 2022 it filed for insolvency that August and wound down.

name: e.GO Mobile
one_liner: Low-cost small city electric car from an Aachen university spinout
story: Professor Günther Schuh, who earlier built the StreetScooter van sold to Deutsche Post, founded e.GO to make cheap city EVs. Production stayed tiny, a planned SPAC listing fell apart, and after a first insolvency in 2020 it filed again in 2024.

name: DaWanda
one_liner: German marketplace for handmade and craft goods
story: DaWanda launched a year after Etsy and became the leading handmade marketplace in German-speaking Europe. As Etsy localised and grew its global network of buyers, DaWanda's growth stalled; it closed in August 2018 and pointed its sellers to Etsy.

name: Qype
one_liner: European local reviews site for restaurants and shops
story: Qype built Europe's biggest Yelp-style reviews community across several countries. Yelp bought it in 2012 for about $50M in cash and stock to enter Europe and then folded the Qype brand into Yelp.

name: Tier Mobility
one_liner: Shared e-scooter and e-bike operator across European cities
story: Tier raced Lime, Voi, Bird and Dott across Europe and hit a $2B valuation in 2021. City tenders, bans like Paris's 2023 vote and price wars squeezed margins; in 2024 it merged into rival Dott at a fraction of its peak value.

name: Home24
one_liner: Rocket Internet's online furniture and home retailer
story: Home24 was a Rocket Internet clone of Wayfair for Germany and Brazil and listed in Frankfurt in 2018. Bulky-goods logistics and thin margins kept it loss-making; furniture giant XXXLutz took it over in 2023 at a share price far below the IPO price.

name: ComROAD
one_liner: Vehicle telematics and navigation company on Germany's Neuer Markt
story: ComROAD was a Neuer Markt star after its 1999 IPO, reporting fast-growing sales of traffic-telematics systems. In 2002 it emerged that about 97% of its revenue came from a fictitious Hong Kong customer; the CEO was convicted and the company collapsed.

name: BlaBlaCar
one_liner: Long-distance carpooling marketplace matching drivers with passengers sharing costs

rounds.lead: Insight Venture Partners, Lead Edge Capital

story: BlaBlaCar spent years before finding a business model (booking fees), then grew across Europe, Russia, India and Latin America, buying German rival Carpooling.com in 2015. A $200M round in 2015 valued it at $1.6B, and it later added buses (OuiBus, Busfor). In the US, long-distance carpooling startup Zimride never scaled and its team pivoted to Lyft.

name: Doctolib
one_liner: Online doctor appointment booking plus practice-management software
story: Doctolib charges doctors a monthly subscription for scheduling software and gives patients free online booking, spreading across France, Germany and Italy. It ran France's COVID vaccine bookings and raised €500M in 2022 at €5.8B (~$6.1B).

name: Mistral AI
one_liner: European foundation-model lab releasing open-weight and commercial LLMs
story: Founded by ex-DeepMind and Meta researchers, Mistral raised a then-record €105M seed four weeks after founding in 2023. Positioned as Europe's sovereign AI champion, it raised €1.7B led by chipmaker ASML in 2025 at €11.7B (~$13.7B).

name: Criteo
one_liner: Ad retargeting platform showing shoppers products they viewed
story: Criteo pivoted from movie recommendations to retargeting ads paid per click and listed on Nasdaq in 2013, raising about $250M at roughly $1.7B. It later suffered as Apple and Google restricted third-party cookies and tracking.

name: Alan
one_liner: Digital health insurer for companies and their employees
story: Alan became the first new French insurer licensed in decades and sells top-up health cover through employers in France, Belgium and Spain. A €173M round led by Belfius in 2024 valued it at €4B (~$4.3B).

name: Ÿnsect
one_liner: Industrial-scale mealworm farming for animal feed and fertiliser
story: Ÿnsect raised one of the largest agri-food rounds ever ($372M Series C in 2020) to build a giant automated insect farm in Amiens. The plant overran costs while insect meal stayed pricier than fishmeal and soy; it entered receivership in 2024 and was ordered into liquidation in 2025.

name: Sigfox
one_liner: Low-power global network for cheap IoT sensor connectivity
story: Sigfox raised €150M in 2016, then France's largest tech round, to build a global '0G' network for IoT devices. Volumes stayed far below forecasts as telcos pushed NB-IoT/LTE-M and LoRa spread; it entered receivership in January 2022 and was bought by Singapore's UnaBiz.

name: Luko
one_liner: Digital home and renters insurance with app-based claims
story: Luko grew fast selling home insurance online in France, Spain and Germany. High claims costs and losses led its carrier and regulators to step in; it entered receivership in late 2023, Allianz Direct took over the policies and German insurtech Getsafe bought the company in early 2024.

name: Adyen
one_liner: Single global payments platform for large merchants, built on its own stack
story: Adyen's founders had already sold payments firm Bibit and rebuilt payments as one in-house platform, winning clients like Uber, Spotify and eBay. Profitable early, it raised little and listed in Amsterdam in 2018 at about €7.1B (~$8.4B), roughly doubling on day one.

name: Booking.com
one_liner: Online hotel booking site charging hotels commission (agency model)
story: Started as Bookings.nl in Amsterdam, it let independent European hotels pay commission only on stays rather than pre-buying rooms. Priceline bought it in 2005 for $133M, and it became the core of what is now Booking Holdings, worth well over $100B.

name: Picnic
one_liner: App-only supermarket delivering free in fixed slots with small electric vans
story: Picnic delivers groceries free in pre-set 20-minute windows on fixed neighbourhood routes, like a milkman, keeping vans full. It expanded slowly into Germany and France and raised €600M in 2022 and €355M in 2024 (Edeka-led), the opposite approach to 10-minute dark-store apps.

name: Hyves
one_liner: Dutch social network that dominated the Netherlands before Facebook
story: Hyves had more Dutch users than Facebook in the late 2000s and was sold to Telegraaf Media Groep in 2010 for about €44M (~$59M). Facebook overtook it within two years and the social network shut in December 2013.

name: VanMoof
one_liner: Design-led direct-to-consumer e-bikes with proprietary parts
story: VanMoof sold sleek e-bikes direct with custom parts only it could repair, and raised $128M in 2021 during the pandemic bike boom. Repair backlogs, supply-chain costs and selling bikes below cost drained cash; it went bankrupt in July 2023 and was bought by Lavoie, a McLaren Applied company.

name: Lightyear
one_liner: Long-range solar electric car from an Eindhoven solar-racing team
story: Lightyear built the Lightyear 0, a solar car priced around €250,000, planning a cheaper mass-market model later. It could not fund production of the second car and its main operating company went bankrupt in January 2023; a smaller successor now sells solar roof technology.

name: Take Eat Easy
one_liner: Restaurant delivery service using bike couriers in European cities
story: Take Eat Easy expanded to cities in Belgium, France, Spain and Germany but could not close a new round against far better-funded Deliveroo, Foodora and Uber Eats. It entered receivership in July 2016, leaving couriers and restaurants unpaid; its founder's public post-mortem became a classic.

name: Lernout & Hauspie
one_liner: Speech-recognition and translation software company
story: Lernout & Hauspie was Belgium's tech champion of the 1990s, buying Dragon Systems and others to lead speech recognition. In 2000 the Wall Street Journal exposed fake revenue in its Korean unit; it went bankrupt, its founders were later convicted and its technology passed to ScanSoft, later Nuance.

name: Kazaa
one_liner: Peer-to-peer file-sharing app used to swap music and video
story: Built by Niklas Zennström and Janus Friis with Estonian developers, Kazaa became one of the most downloaded programs in the world after Napster's fall. Lawsuits from music and film companies led its owner to pay about $100M in a 2006 settlement and the service faded; its founders reused the P2P tech to create Skype.

name: Joost
one_liner: Internet TV service from the Skype founders using peer-to-peer streaming
story: Joost raised $45M from CBS, Viacom, Sequoia and Index to stream licensed TV through a downloadable P2P app. Users preferred YouTube and Hulu in the browser and studios held back content; it abandoned its app in 2008 and was sold to ad network Adconion in 2009.

name: OneCoin
one_liner: Fake cryptocurrency sold through multi-level marketing 'education packages'
story: OneCoin claimed to be a bitcoin rival but had no real blockchain; it sold packages to millions of investors through MLM networks, raising about $4B according to US prosecutors. Founder Ruja Ignatova vanished in 2017 and remains on the FBI's most-wanted list; co-founder Sebastian Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years.

name: Glovo
one_liner: On-demand courier app delivering anything from local stores and restaurants in under 30 minutes
story: Glovo started in Barcelona delivering 'anything' and won Spain, Italy, Portugal, Eastern Europe and Africa where it arrived first. It lost Latin America to the better-funded Rappi and sold those operations to Delivery Hero in 2020 for about €230M (~$272M); Delivery Hero then took majority control in 2022 valuing Glovo at €2.3B (~$2.4B). Spain's 2021 rider law forced it toward employing couriers by 2025.

name: Cabify
one_liner: Ride-hailing app using licensed private-hire drivers in Spain and Latin America
story: Cabify launched in Madrid in 2011 using licensed VTC drivers and expanded early into Latin America, absorbing Easy Taxi in 2017. When Uber was banned from Spain in 2014 Cabify kept growing, and a Rakuten-led $160M round in 2018 made it Spain's first unicorn.

name: Wallapop
one_liner: Mobile app for buying and selling second-hand goods locally
story: Wallapop won Spain's second-hand market and in 2016 absorbed the Spanish operations of rival Letgo, which then focused (and failed) in the US. It added shipping and a protection fee model and raised €157M in 2021 at about €690M (~$815M) from Naver-backed Korelya.

name: Letgo
one_liner: Barcelona-built second-hand marketplace app that bet on the US market
story: Letgo was built in Barcelona by OLX founder Alec Oxenford and others and raised close to $1B, mostly from Naspers, to take on OfferUp and Craigslist in the US with heavy TV advertising. Facebook Marketplace launched in 2016 and squeezed it; in 2020 Letgo's US business was merged into OfferUp and the app shut down.

name: Jobandtalent
one_liner: Digital temp-staffing agency matching workers with warehouse, logistics and retail shifts
story: Jobandtalent started as a job board, then became a tech-run temp agency that employs workers directly, avoiding the gig-classification fights hitting Uber and Glovo. E-commerce logistics demand during COVID drove a $500M SoftBank-led round in 2021 at $2.35B.

name: Idealista
one_liner: Spain's leading online property listings portal, also in Italy and Portugal
story: Founded by the Encinar brothers during the dot-com boom, Idealista became the dominant Spanish property portal and expanded to Italy and Portugal. It passed between private-equity owners (Apax, then EQT for €1.3B in 2020) and Cinven bought it in 2024 for €2.9B (~$3.1B).

name: TravelPerk
one_liner: Business travel booking and management platform for companies
story: TravelPerk survived COVID wiping out business travel, then rode the rebound to a $1.3B valuation in a SoftBank-led round in 2022. It raised a further $200M in 2025 and kept expanding in the US.

name: Factorial
one_liner: HR software for small and mid-sized businesses
story: Factorial started with free HR software for small companies in Spain and upsold paid modules, expanding to Latin America and the US. A $120M Series C led by Atomico in 2022 made it a unicorn.

name: Tuenti
one_liner: Invite-only Spanish social network popular with teenagers
story: Founded by American Zaryn Dentzel in Madrid, Tuenti was Spain's biggest social network for teens and Telefónica bought it in 2010 for about €70M (~$93M). Facebook overtook it within a few years and Telefónica turned Tuenti into a mobile operator brand, closing the social network in 2016.

name: Social Point
one_liner: Barcelona mobile game studio behind Dragon City and Monster Legends
story: Social Point built free-to-play hits Dragon City and Monster Legends on Facebook and then mobile. Take-Two Interactive bought it in 2017 for $250M ($175M cash plus stock), one of Spain's largest tech exits at the time.

name: Privalia
one_liner: Members-only flash-sale site for discounted fashion brands
story: Privalia copied France's vente-privée flash-sales model for Spain, Italy, Brazil and Mexico. Vente-privée bought it in 2016 for €500M (~$555M), while US flash-sale star Gilt Groupe sold that year for about $250M after reaching a $1B valuation.

name: Terra Networks
one_liner: Telefónica's Spanish-language internet portal and ISP of the dot-com boom
story: Terra listed in Madrid and on Nasdaq in November 1999 and its shares soared more than tenfold within months; in 2000 it bought US portal Lycos for $12.5B in stock. When the bubble burst the value evaporated and Telefónica reabsorbed Terra in 2005 at a fraction of its peak.

name: OutSystems
one_liner: Low-code platform for building enterprise applications quickly
story: OutSystems grew slowly for 17 years in Portugal before KKR and Goldman Sachs invested $360M in 2018, making it Portugal's first unicorn. A 2021 round valued it at $9.5B as low-code became a hot category.

name: Spotify
one_liner: Freemium music streaming licensed from the record labels
story: Spotify launched in Sweden in 2008, where piracy (The Pirate Bay, Kazaa) had gutted music sales, offering labels a legal alternative and equity stakes. It took three years to get US licences, then won globally and did a direct listing on the NYSE in 2018 at about $26.5B.

name: Klarna
one_liner: Buy-now-pay-later checkout and shopping app
story: Klarna started in 2005 letting Swedes pay online by invoice after delivery, then became Europe's BNPL leader with a banking licence for cheap funding. Valued at $45.6B in 2021, it raised at just $6.7B in 2022 as rates rose, then listed on the NYSE in September 2025 at about $15B.

name: Supercell
one_liner: Mobile game studio of small autonomous teams (Clash of Clans, Brawl Stars)
story: Supercell kills most games in testing and lets tiny teams ship only big hits like Hay Day and Clash of Clans. SoftBank bought 51% for $1.5B in 2013 and Tencent bought 84% in 2016 at a $10.2B valuation.

name: Mojang
one_liner: Indie studio behind Minecraft, bootstrapped from game sales
story: Markus Persson sold Minecraft while it was still in alpha and funded Mojang entirely from sales, turning down VC. Microsoft bought Mojang in 2014 for $2.5B.

name: iZettle
one_liner: Mobile card reader and point-of-sale app for small merchants
story: iZettle brought Square's idea to Europe with chip-and-PIN readers and spread across Europe and Latin America. PayPal bought it for $2.2B in 2018, days before its planned IPO.

name: Wolt
one_liner: Food and retail delivery app focused on smaller European cities
story: Wolt won the Nordics, Baltics and Central Europe by going to cities competitors ignored and obsessing over service. DoorDash agreed to buy it in November 2021 for €7B (~$8.1B) in stock, its biggest international bet; the value fell with DoorDash's share price before closing in 2022.

name: Skype
one_liner: Free internet voice and video calls using peer-to-peer technology
story: Built by Kazaa's founders with Estonian engineers who wrote the P2P code, Skype offered free calls between computers and paid calls to phones. eBay bought it in 2005 for $2.6B and Microsoft paid $8.5B in 2011; its alumni seeded Estonia's startup scene (Wise, Bolt).

name: MySQL AB
one_liner: Company behind the open-source MySQL database
story: MySQL became the default database of the early web through free open-source distribution, earning money from dual licences and support. Sun Microsystems bought MySQL AB for $1B in 2008, a landmark open-source exit.

name: Northvolt
one_liner: European champion building lithium-ion battery gigafactories
story: Founded by ex-Tesla executive Peter Carlsson, Northvolt raised over $15B in equity and debt from Volkswagen, Goldman Sachs and governments to rival Chinese battery makers. Its Skellefteå plant struggled with production yields, BMW cancelled a €2B order in 2024, and it filed for Chapter 11 in November 2024 and Swedish bankruptcy in March 2025.

name: Volta Trucks
one_liner: Purpose-built electric trucks for city deliveries
story: Volta Trucks designed the Volta Zero city truck and began production in Austria in 2023. When its battery supplier Proterra filed for bankruptcy, production stalled and Volta filed for bankruptcy in October 2023.

name: Bolt
one_liner: Lower-cost ride-hailing, scooter and delivery super-app (formerly Taxify)
story: Founded by teenager Markus Villig as Taxify, it undercut Uber's commissions in Eastern Europe and Africa. Its 2017 London launch was shut down by the regulator within days for lacking a licence, but it relaunched in 2019 and raised €628M in 2022 at €7.4B (~$7.8B).

name: Vinted
one_liner: Peer-to-peer marketplace for second-hand clothes with no seller fees
story: Vinted began in Lithuania in 2008, moved fees from sellers to buyers and built integrated shipping, then won France, Germany and much of Europe. Valued at €3.5B in 2021, it turned profitable in 2023 and a 2024 secondary valued it at €5B (~$5.4B).

name: UiPath
one_liner: Robotic process automation software that automates repetitive office tasks
story: Daniel Dines started UiPath as an outsourcing shop in Bucharest before pivoting to automation software, later moving headquarters to New York. It reached a $35B private valuation and listed on the NYSE in April 2021 at about $29B, Romania's biggest tech success.

name: Runtastic
one_liner: Fitness and running-tracking apps
story: Four Austrians built a family of running and fitness apps with tens of millions of downloads. Adidas bought Runtastic in 2015 for €220M (~$244M) to own a digital fitness platform.

name: GoStudent
one_liner: Online one-to-one tutoring marketplace for school students
story: GoStudent became Europe's most valuable edtech after a €300M round in 2022 at €3B (~$3.15B) backed by DST, Tencent and SoftBank. After schools reopened, growth slowed and it cut staff and wrote down acquisitions, but kept operating unlike India's BYJU'S.

name: Bitpanda
one_liner: Retail platform for buying crypto, stocks and metals under EU licences
story: Bitpanda was profitable early and collected EU financial licences before most crypto rivals, helping it survive the 2022 crash. A Valar-led $263M round in 2021 valued it at $4.1B.

name: Avast
one_liner: Freemium consumer antivirus software
story: Avast gave antivirus away free to hundreds of millions of users and sold premium upgrades, listing in London in 2018. NortonLifeLock bought it in 2022 for about $8.6B, after a 2020 scandal over its Jumpshot unit selling browsing data.

name: JetBrains
one_liner: Developer IDEs (IntelliJ, PyCharm) and the Kotlin language, built without VC
story: Three engineers started JetBrains in Prague in 2000 and grew it with paid developer tools, never raising outside capital. Its Kotlin language became Google's preferred language for Android in 2019.

name: Wix
one_liner: Drag-and-drop website builder for small businesses
story: Wix started as a Flash-based site builder and rebuilt on HTML5 as Flash died, converting free users into premium plans at scale. It listed on Nasdaq in November 2013, raising about $127M, and grew into a multi-billion-dollar company with hundreds of millions of registered users.

name: Mobileye
one_liner: Camera-based driver-assistance chips and computer vision for carmakers
story: Professor Amnon Shashua's Mobileye spent a decade getting its vision chips designed into cars, then had the largest Israeli IPO on the NYSE in 2014 at about $5.3B. Intel bought it in 2017 for $15.3B and spun it back out in a 2022 IPO.

name: Waze
one_liner: Crowdsourced real-time traffic and navigation app
story: Waze turned drivers' phones into traffic sensors and let users edit the map, building data Google and Apple lacked. After talks with Facebook and Apple, Google bought it in June 2013 for about $1.1B, having raised about $67M.

name: monday.com
one_liner: Visual work-management platform for teams
story: Started as an internal tool at Wix, monday.com (originally dapulse) grew with heavy online advertising into a horizontal work OS. It was valued at $1.9B in 2019 and listed on Nasdaq in June 2021 at about $6.8B.

name: Wiz
one_liner: Agentless cloud security platform scanning entire cloud environments
story: Wiz's founders had sold Adallom to Microsoft and built Wiz into the fastest software company to $100M ARR. After rejecting a $23B Google offer in 2024, it agreed in March 2025 to be acquired by Google for $32B in cash, Israel's largest ever tech deal.

name: Moovit
one_liner: Public-transit journey planner covering thousands of cities
story: Moovit used crowdsourcing and local volunteer 'Mooviters' to map transit in far more cities than rivals like Citymapper. Intel bought it in 2020 for about $900M to pair with Mobileye's robotaxi plans.

name: Fiverr
one_liner: Marketplace for freelance services, originally all priced at $5
story: Fiverr packaged freelance work as fixed-price 'gigs' starting at $5, making services browsable like products. It listed on the NYSE in June 2019 raising about $111M and boomed during the remote-work era of 2020-21 before falling back.

name: Mirabilis (ICQ)
one_liner: ICQ, one of the first mass-market internet instant messengers
story: Four young Israelis and investor Yossi Vardi launched ICQ in 1996 and it reached tens of millions of users without revenue. AOL bought Mirabilis in 1998 for $407M, a landmark exit that helped launch Israel's startup ecosystem.

name: ironSource
one_liner: Mobile app monetisation and advertising platform for game developers
story: ironSource went public via a Thoma Bravo SPAC in 2021 at about $11.1B, one of the few profitable SPAC listings. After Apple's privacy changes hit mobile ads it merged into Unity in 2022 in an all-stock deal worth about $4.4B.

name: Better Place
one_liner: EV charging and battery-swap network selling 'miles' like a mobile plan
story: Shai Agassi raised about $850M to build battery-swap stations in Israel and Denmark, with Renault as the only carmaker making a compatible car. Fewer than 1,000 cars were sold in Israel, costs ballooned and it went bankrupt in May 2013; China's NIO later made battery swapping work by owning both car and battery.

name: Careem
one_liner: Middle East ride-hailing app built for local payment and safety norms
story: Careem started as a corporate car booking service and adapted ride-hailing to the region with cash payments and local drivers, beating Uber in many Middle Eastern and Pakistani cities. Uber bought it for $3.1B ($1.7B in convertible notes and $1.4B cash), closing in January 2020, the region's largest tech deal at the time.

name: Talabat
one_liner: Gulf food and grocery delivery leader
story: Founded in Kuwait in 2004, long before smartphones, Talabat was sold to Rocket Internet in 2015 for $170M and then folded into Delivery Hero. In December 2024 it listed in Dubai raising about $2B at roughly $10.2B, the world's biggest tech IPO that year.

name: Souq.com
one_liner: The Arab world's largest e-commerce marketplace, later Amazon.ae
story: Souq grew out of Jordanian web group Maktoob and built its own delivery and cash-on-delivery network across the Gulf and Egypt. Valued around $1B in 2016 as the region's first unicorn, it was bought by Amazon in 2017 for about $580M.

name: Swvl
one_liner: App-booked shared buses on fixed commuter routes in emerging-market cities
story: Swvl offered cheap, reliable bus seats for Cairo commuters and expanded to Kenya, Pakistan, Latin America and Europe, listing via SPAC in March 2022 at about $1.5B. It then cut over half its staff, exited markets and failed acquisitions; by March 2023 its shares were down over 99%, leaving a market value near $9M.

name: Anghami
one_liner: Arabic-first music streaming service
story: Anghami launched in Beirut in 2012, years before Spotify entered the Middle East, licensing Arabic catalogues and billing through telcos. It became the first Arab tech company to list on Nasdaq via a 2022 SPAC at roughly $220M; OSN+ later took majority control.

name: InstaDeep
one_liner: Tunisian-founded AI company building decision-making and biology AI
story: Karim Beguir and Zohra Slim started InstaDeep in Tunis in 2014 with two laptops and about $2,000, later moving headquarters to London. After a $100M Series B in 2022, BioNTech bought it in 2023 for up to £562M (~$682M), Africa's largest AI exit.

name: Maktoob
one_liner: First Arabic-language email service and web portal
story: Samih Toukan and Hussam Khoury built Arabic webmail and a portal in Amman. Yahoo bought Maktoob in 2009 for about $164M, the Arab world's first big tech exit, and its founders spun off Souq.com, later sold to Amazon.

name: Tabby
one_liner: Buy-now-pay-later and shopping app for Saudi Arabia and the UAE
story: Tabby launched in the UAE in 2019 with interest-free pay-in-4 and moved its HQ to Riyadh as Saudi Arabia pushed digital payments. It became a unicorn in 2023 and was valued at $3.3B in 2025, while African BNPL Lipa Later went into administration.

name: Kitopi
one_liner: Cloud kitchen operator cooking for partner restaurant brands
story: Kitopi runs shared kitchens that cook for established restaurant brands (and its own) across the Gulf, using software to manage many menus in one kitchen. SoftBank led a $415M round in 2021 that made it a unicorn, while many US and African cloud-kitchen startups shut.

name: Fawry
one_liner: Egypt's electronic bill-payment network running through retail agents
story: Fawry let Egyptians pay bills and government fees in cash at hundreds of thousands of shops and points, digitising payments in a cash economy. Its 2019 listing on the Egyptian Exchange was heavily oversubscribed and its market value later crossed $1B, Egypt's first tech unicorn.

name: Fetchr
one_liner: Courier app delivering to a phone's GPS location instead of a street address
story: Fetchr solved the Gulf's lack of street addresses by delivering to a smartphone's location, raising NEA's first Middle East investment and a 2017 round at almost $300M valuation. After nearly collapsing in 2019 it pivoted to Saudi Arabia, where a disputed ~$100M VAT and zakat bill left it insolvent in 2021.

name: Capiter
one_liner: B2B e-commerce supplying Egyptian corner shops with groceries and goods
story: Capiter raised a $33M Series A in 2021 to digitise ordering for Egypt's informal retailers and expanded into Saudi Arabia. In September 2022 the board fired the founder brothers amid financial-mismanagement allegations (denied and never proven in court), leaving the company in arrears to staff and creditors.

name: Getir
one_liner: Turkish pioneer of 10-minute grocery delivery from dark stores
story: Getir invented 10-minute delivery in Istanbul in 2015, where dense neighbourhoods and lower wages made it work, and was valued at $11.8B in 2022. Its international expansion failed and it quit all markets outside Turkey by 2024; its valuation fell to about $2.5B and Mubadala took control of the core Turkish business.

name: Trendyol
one_liner: Turkey's largest e-commerce marketplace, majority-owned by Alibaba
story: Demet Mutlu started Trendyol as a fashion flash-sales site and turned it into Turkey's dominant marketplace with its own delivery and food/grocery arms. Alibaba bought a majority in 2018 and a $1.5B round in 2021 valued it at $16.5B, Turkey's most valuable startup.

name: Peak Games
one_liner: Istanbul mobile game studio behind Toon Blast and Toy Blast
story: Peak Games started with Turkish card games and then hit global success with casual puzzlers Toy Blast and Toon Blast. Zynga bought it in 2020 for $1.8B, then Turkey's largest tech exit, and Peak alumni founded Dream Games.

name: Yemeksepeti
one_liner: Turkey's pioneering online food ordering platform
story: Nevzat Aydın launched Yemeksepeti for web food ordering in 2001, a decade before smartphones, and built a profitable marketplace across Turkey and the Gulf. Delivery Hero bought it in 2015 for $589M, a record Turkish internet deal at the time.

name: WhereIsMyTransport
one_liner: Mapping data for informal minibus-taxi networks in emerging-market cities
story: WhereIsMyTransport mapped the informal minibus and paratransit routes that most commuters in African and Latin American cities rely on, selling data and a commuter app. It was among the high-profile African closures of 2023 as venture funding dried up.

name: Jumia Food
one_liner: Jumia's restaurant food-delivery service across seven African countries
story: Started under Rocket Internet's Hellofood brand and later run as Jumia Food, the service offered restaurant delivery in Nigeria, Kenya, Morocco and four other markets. Low order values and high delivery costs kept it loss-making and Jumia shut it in all seven countries in December 2023 to focus on e-commerce.

name: Exscientia
one_liner: AI-driven drug discovery company designing small-molecule drugs
story: Exscientia put what it called the first AI-designed drug molecule into clinical trials in 2020 and listed on Nasdaq in 2021. Pipeline setbacks and the 2024 dismissal of its founder-CEO preceded an all-stock merger into US rival Recursion in 2024 valuing it at about $688M, well below its IPO-era value.

name: Starship Technologies
one_liner: Six-wheeled sidewalk robots for autonomous last-mile deliveries
story: Skype co-founders Ahti Heinla and Janus Friis started Starship to make deliveries with small sidewalk robots, built in Estonia. It found traction on US university campuses and European suburbs where routes are short and predictable, and has completed millions of deliveries.

name: Gymshark
one_liner: Direct-to-consumer gym clothing brand built on social-media influencers
story: Ben Francis started Gymshark at 19, sewing clothes and sponsoring early YouTube fitness creators, and grew it without outside capital. General Atlantic bought 21% in 2020, valuing it at over £1B (~$1.3B), unlike UK D2C peer Made.com which collapsed in 2022.

name: Zoopla
one_liner: UK property listings portal with free home valuations
story: Alex Chesterman launched Zoopla in 2007 with free home-value estimates and became the No. 2 UK property portal, listing in London in 2014 at about £919M (~$1.5B). Silver Lake bought its parent ZPG in 2018 for £2.2B (~$2.9B); Chesterman's next company, Cazoo, collapsed in 2024.

name: Bitstamp
one_liner: One of the oldest licensed bitcoin exchanges, started in Slovenia
story: Two Slovenians founded Bitstamp in 2011 as a European alternative to Mt. Gox and it survived a 2015 hack and several crypto crashes by securing licences early. Korean group NXC bought it in 2018 and Robinhood acquired it for about $200M, closing in 2025.

name: Helsing
one_liner: AI software and drones for European defence ministries
story: Helsing sells AI battlefield software and strike drones to European governments, a category VCs avoided until Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Spotify founder Daniel Ek's fund led its 2025 €600M round at €12B (~$13.6B), making it one of Europe's most valuable startups.

name: YOOX (YOOX Net-a-Porter)
one_liner: Online retailer of designer fashion that merged with Net-a-Porter
story: Federico Marchetti launched YOOX in Bologna in 2000 selling off-season designer clothes online, survived the dot-com crash and listed in Milan in 2009. It merged with Net-a-Porter in 2015 and Richemont bought out the rest in 2018; Richemont later sold the business to Mytheresa in 2025 at a steep loss.

name: Satispay
one_liner: Mobile payment network linked to bank accounts, bypassing card fees for merchants
story: Satispay lets Italians pay shops from an app linked to their bank account, with far lower merchant fees than cards, in one of Europe's most cash-heavy countries. A €320M round led by Addition in 2022 put its valuation around €1B, Italy's first fintech unicorn.

name: InPost
one_liner: Network of 24/7 parcel lockers for e-commerce deliveries
story: Rafał Brzoska built a dense network of parcel lockers across Poland, making e-commerce delivery cheaper and faster than couriers to the door. After Advent took it private in 2017, InPost listed in Amsterdam in January 2021 at about €8B (~$9.4B) and expanded into the UK and France.
